speakable_v2.hook: High coupling is why changing a database class breaks five other classes you weren't thinking about.

beats.content: Coupling measures how dependent one class is on another. High coupling means a change in one class ripples through many others. Low coupling means classes can change independently. The goal is loose coupling.

Tight coupling in Java looks like this: OrderService creates a new EmailService inside itself. It now knows the concrete class, it's locked to it, and swapping EmailService for SMSService means editing OrderService. That's the ripple effect.

non-obvious: the main tool for reducing coupling is interfaces. OrderService depending on a NotificationService interface doesn't know or care what's behind it. Spring Boot's entire dependency injection system is built on this idea. You're writing loose coupling every time you inject an interface.

speakable_v2.cap: Low coupling: classes can change independently. Achieve it by depending on interfaces, not concrete classes.

The goal is **loose coupling**: depend through interfaces, minimize direct knowledge of other classes.

question: What is cohesion in software design?
title: Cohesion — what it is and why high cohesion is desirable
direct_answer: **Cohesion** measures how **focused** a class is — how closely related its methods and responsibilities are. **High cohesion** means everything in the class belongs together and serves one purpose. **Low cohesion** means the class is a grab-bag of unrelated things. High cohesion is the goal — it makes classes easier to understand and maintain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding cohesion as the inward-focused metric (how related are the parts of this class)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing cohesion with coupling — coupling is about relationships between classes, cohesion is about internal focus of one class

sections.title: High vs low cohesion
sections.content: High cohesion: UserService has methods like createUser, updateUser, deleteUser, findUser — all related to user management. Low cohesion: UtilityService has sendEmail, calculateTax, generateReport, validateAddress — all unrelated methods crammed into one class. The low cohesion class has no clear identity. High cohesion classes have a clear single purpose.

A UserService with methods to create, find, update, and delete users is highly cohesive — everything belongs together. High cohesion makes classes easier to understand and name, and naturally limits their size.

question: What is the relationship between coupling and cohesion?
title: Coupling and cohesion — the dual metrics of good design
direct_answer: The ideal design has **high cohesion** (each class is focused on one thing) and **low coupling** (classes depend on each other minimally). They are complementary: highly cohesive classes naturally have fewer reasons to depend on other classes, which reduces coupling. The famous formula is: **high cohesion + low coupling = good design**.

beats.content: A God Class does everything: user management, order processing, payment, email, reporting, all in one class. It has low cohesion because nothing inside it is related. It has high coupling because the entire codebase depends on it.

question: What is a God Class and how does it violate cohesion and coupling?
title: God Class antipattern — low cohesion and high coupling
direct_answer: A **God Class** is a class that knows too much and does too much — it is the central hub of the entire application. It has **low cohesion** (does everything) and creates **high coupling** (everything depends on it). Changing it is dangerous because breaking it breaks the whole system. It is the opposite of good design.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not being able to articulate why God Class is bad beyond it is too big

sections.title: Why God Classes are dangerous
sections.content: A God Class has 1000+ lines, handles user management, order processing, payment, email, reporting, and authentication all in one place. It violates SRP (many reasons to change), cohesion (unrelated methods), and is highly coupled to everything. Every feature is tangled with every other feature. You cannot test, change, or deploy any one piece without risking all the others.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: A God Class is the worst-case design antipattern. It is one class that does everything — user management, order processing, payment, email. It violates SRP because it has a hundred reasons to change. It has low cohesion because nothing inside it is related. And it creates high coupling because the entire codebase depends on it. The fix is to break it apart by responsibility — extract UserService, OrderService, PaymentService, and so on.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: Program to an interface, not an implementation is one of the oldest and most practical rules in object-oriented design.

beats.content: Interfaces reduce coupling by inserting an indirection layer. Instead of PaymentService depending directly on StripePayment, it depends on a PaymentGateway interface. StripePayment and PayPalPayment both implement the interface. PaymentService knows neither of them.
The result: swapping Stripe for PayPal means adding a new class that implements PaymentGateway and updating the Spring configuration. PaymentService is untouched. That's loose coupling in practice.

non-obvious: decoupling is also what makes unit tests fast. When PaymentService depends on an interface, tests inject a mock implementation. No real payment gateway is called. This daily testing benefit is worth emphasizing when you talk about loose coupling.

speakable_v2.cap: Interfaces decouple by hiding the implementation. You can swap, extend, or mock without touching the class that depends on the interface.

question: How do interfaces reduce coupling between classes?
title: Interfaces as a tool for reducing coupling in Java
direct_answer: Interfaces reduce coupling by introducing an **indirection layer**. Instead of class A directly depending on class B, A depends on interface I, and B implements I. A does not know B exists — it only knows I. You can swap B for any other implementation of I without touching A. This is **program to interfaces, not implementations**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of how interfaces decouple in Java
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking interfaces are just for multiple implementations — their primary value is decoupling
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect to the famous GoF principle: program to an interface, not an implementation

sections.title: Interface as decoupling layer
How to say this in an interview
sections.content: Interfaces reduce coupling by creating an indirection layer. When PaymentService depends on a PaymentGateway interface instead of Stripe directly, it has no knowledge of Stripe. I can swap in PayPal, Razorpay, or a mock without changing PaymentService at all. This is the GoF principle: program to an interface, not an implementation. In Spring Boot this is the default way of working — services depend on interfaces, implementations are injected.
